Rethink your security response strategies; AI has fundamentally changed the game.

stories.title: KHMS a file-based long-term memory for LLM agents
stories.social_post:
Building effective long-term memory for LLM agents is one of the toughest challenges in agentic AI. Most solutions rely on vector databases, but what if you could use something simpler and more auditable?

Introducing KHMS, a "know-how management system" that leverages plain markdown files in a Git repository. Each piece of knowledge is an immutable card with YAML frontmatter, allowing corrections through new, superseding cards rather than edits.

This system includes a hook-driven recall mechanism to push relevant cards into the agent's session and a propose-review-approve pipeline for human oversight. It is an agent's self-installable, auditable memory that operates like a personal knowledge base.

This innovative, production-tested design offers a highly practical and transparent approach to agent memory, enhancing reliability and control.

stories.title: PEP 805 proposes safe parallel execution in CPython by default
stories.social_post:
Free-threading in Python has long faced a harsh trade-off between concurrency throughput and memory safety. PEP 805 attacks this problem at the language runtime layer by introducing ThreadGroups and an explicit Sharing Xor Mutability model.

Under this proposal, parallel Python execution becomes race-free by default. Mutable objects cannot cross thread boundaries unless developers explicitly freeze them or encapsulate them in synchronized wrappers. This design shifts the synchronization burden away from pervasive fine-grained locking and toward structural isolation.

CPython avoids the high overhead of atomic reference counting on every single operation by partitioning heaps across thread groups. The runtime can reclaim deferred memory safely while letting worker threads execute true parallel computations across multiple CPU cores without race hazards.

Enforcing mutability discipline at the runtime level solves the hardest concurrency bugs before code reaches production.
stories.why_read: Understand how CPython intends to achieve race-free thread parallelism by separating mutability and sharing.

stories.title: Claude Code Opus 5 Auto Mode vulnerable to prompt injection code execution
stories.social_post:
Auto Mode in agentic coding tools cannot replace isolated OS-level sandboxing, no matter how confident safety classifier benchmarks appear.

A recent evaluation of Claude Code Opus 5 claimed a zero percent prompt injection success rate in Auto Mode across dozens of scenarios. However, a targeted indirect attack achieved an eighty percent exploit success rate by exploiting tool orchestration and standard operating system behavior.

The exploit chain avoids obvious dangerous shell commands. An attacker tricks the agent into downloading and extracting a zip archive. Claude inspects the files, refuses to run an untrusted compiled binary, and instead writes a safe Python script to decode the payload.

The catastrophic flaw occurs when Claude executes that Python script directly inside the untrusted directory. Python automatically places the working directory at the front of the module search path. The directory contains a poisoned struct.py file. As soon as the script imports standard libraries like base64, Python loads the local malicious struct module and executes arbitrary attacker code.

Software harnesses must isolate file execution paths and virtual environments rather than relying on LLM intent classifiers to catch multistep exploitation.
stories.why_read: Learn how attacker-controlled directories weaponize standard Python import resolution against autonomous coding agents. You will discover why safety classifiers fail to replace hardened execution sandboxes.

stories.title: Addressing LDS Layout and Partition Conflicts Optimizes AMD MI450 GPU Performance
stories.social_post:
In high-performance GEMM kernels on AMD Instinct hardware, the throughput of matrix cores is frequently constrained not by raw arithmetic capacity, but by how operands move through Local Data Share memory.

Two subtle hardware bottlenecks quietly degrade performance. When an in-memory layout fails to match the wave matrix-multiply-accumulate requirements, such as an N-contiguous operand requiring K-contiguous alignment, vectorization breaks completely. Engineers can restore full vector loads by leveraging cooperative-transpose instructions like ds_load_tr to reorder data in flight.

The second bottleneck stems from physical partition conflicts. When warps reading from Local Data Share hit the exact same memory partition through competing ports, accesses serialize. Resolving this requires restructuring the layout to physically distribute data across partitions, enabling parallel memory access across wave fronts.

Optimizing memory layout before touching compute instructions is how engineers extract peak performance from modern accelerators.
stories.why_read: This article explains how to optimize LDS performance on AMD Instinct MI450 GPUs. Readers will learn about transposed LDS loads and how to prevent partition conflicts for better GEMM kernel throughput.

stories.title: Agent swarms create costly distributed systems problems for shared knowledge
stories.social_post:
Traditional database transactions fall apart when applied to collaborative AI agent swarms. In standard relational databases, an aborted transaction is cheap to retry because the engine merely re-executes the exact same deterministic SQL code in a few milliseconds.

Agentic systems change this trade-off completely. When an agent transaction aborts due to a concurrency conflict, the retry requires re-reasoning from scratch. That retry consumes several minutes of wall-clock latency and significant monetary cost in input and output tokens.

Git-style merges fail natural language knowledge bases for a similar reason. Code diffs align well with line-based syntax, but natural prose undergoes summarization, restructuring, and subtle deletions that line diffs destroy. Naive branching strategies end up discarding more completed reasoning work than they preserve.

Building shared state for agent swarms requires optimizing for goodput rather than raw throughput. Distributed system engineers must shift toward semantic merge semantics and conflict avoidance mechanisms that prevent expensive reasoning rollbacks before they occur.

Aborting a transaction should never cost five dollars and three minutes of compute.

stories.title: I accidentally turned LLM memory into program analysis
stories.social_post:
Standard vector retrieval fails for long-horizon agent reasoning because it treats memory as a search problem rather than a state consistency problem. When an agent embeds past observations, it cannot distinguish between valid assumptions and premises that were invalidated ten steps ago.

If an agent learns that an input points to an invalid buffer, it draws downstream conclusions. But if subsequent investigation disproves the initial premise, semantic search still retrieves the old conclusion and feeds it back into context. The agent continues reasoning from an idea that is no longer true.

Applying truth maintenance systems from classical program analysis fixes this defect. Instead of flat conversation chunks, the agent tracks explicit dependency trees. When an upstream assertion gets refuted, all dependent conclusions are automatically pruned from the active state.

Agents do not just need larger context windows; they require rigorous state management that actively invalidates stale beliefs.
stories.why_read: This article explores how current LLM memory systems fail during long vulnerability research sessions. It introduces an innovative approach that effectively transforms LLM memory into a form of program analysis to maintain established facts and prevent models from losing track of prior findings.

stories.title: Don't use musl if you care about performance
stories.social_post:
Compiling services with musl to achieve static, portable container binaries introduces severe latency regressions that cannot be solved by swapping allocators.

Many backend teams assume that the performance penalty of musl is strictly confined to its naive default allocator. Swapping the allocator for jemalloc or mimalloc helps workloads with heavy heap churn, but microbenchmarks show the final binary can still run over twenty-five percent slower than a glibc equivalent.

The deeper problem lies within basic memory routines. Essential operations like memory copying and string searches in musl are written for simplicity and code size rather than throughput. Highly optimized vector routines present in glibc are absent, meaning compute-heavy services that barely allocate still experience measurable degradation.

Static linking simplicity is appealing, but running performance-critical services on musl creates invisible infrastructure bottlenecks.
stories.why_read: This article explains why musl libc can lead to significant performance degradation, even with alternative allocators, and details specific areas of slowness beyond just the allocator. Readers will learn about musl's performance pitfalls compared to glibc and the limitations of simply swapping allocators.

stories.title: Your AI agent running a shell server has root
stories.social_post:

The implications are stark: without explicit sandboxing or privilege separation, a compromised or misbehaving agent could wipe your home directory, deploy malicious code, or access sensitive cloud resources. This is not just a theoretical risk; it is the default state for many current setups.

This finding should immediately push every engineer working with agentic AI to rethink their execution environments. The principle of least privilege is not just a good idea, it is an urgent requirement for AI agents interacting with your system.

stories.title: AI coding bot context files do not improve success rates
stories.social_post:

This observation holds across different LLMs and coding agents, even with human-written context files. It challenges the common belief that more context automatically leads to better performance. Instead, it suggests that agents can get distracted or simply fail to leverage the additional information effectively, leading to wasted tokens and no real gain.

The key takeaway is that better context engineering means being ruthlessly selective, not simply providing more data. This insight is critical for anyone aiming to build truly effective and cost-efficient AI agents, reminding us that sometimes, less is genuinely more.

stories.social_post:

It is not just about logging what happened; ConductAI focuses on controlling what can happen. stories.title: AutoSaddler optimizes LLM agent harnesses using execution traces
stories.social_post:
Most real-world failures in agentic systems do not stem from base model limitations, but from brittle, handcrafted external harnesses. When an agent drifts off course during a long task, errors compound quickly, yet tuning prompts and control flow by hand remains slow and unscientific.

AutoSaddler reframes harness design as an automated offline learning problem. Instead of guessing how to rewrite system prompts or adjust tool schemas, the system diagnoses failure traces from mini-batches and generates structured code patches directly against the harness. It then validates those changes against holdout trajectories to prevent overfitting to specific runs.

Across benchmarks like SWE-Bench Pro, GAIA2, and Terminal-Bench 2.0, this iterative loop produced performance gains between 9.0 and 10.0 percentage points over base harnesses. The key architectural takeaway is that targeted code patches informed by deep execution debugging consistently beat broad prompt rewrites and shallow reflection.

Treating the agent harness as compiled code rather than prompt poetry is how teams will build reliable production agents.

stories.title: alloca ensures large stack allocations do not skip guard page

This is not just about moving a stack pointer. It is about a precise sequence of probes that ensure guard pages are hit, preventing silent memory corruption and system instability. Understanding these mechanics is fundamental, not just for systems engineers, but for anyone debugging complex native applications.

stories.title: Cutting AI coding agent context overhead with dynamic tool activation
stories.social_post:
Most coding agents waste up to 25,000 tokens of context on turn zero before a user even submits a prompt.

Modern agent harnesses commonly register dozens of tools up front, ranging from shell execution to browser automation. On roughly 90 percent of turns, however, an assistant only requires standard file system and shell operations. Injecting 80 tool schemas into every request clutters attention, degrades reasoning, and causes unnecessary inference latency.

Dynamic tool activation solves this problem by maintaining a minimal core set of four active tools while keeping specialized tools on standby. The runtime registers extra tools only when explicitly triggered by the task, applying a time-to-live eviction policy to prune them automatically once completed.

Telemetry across 10,000 turns demonstrates that this approach slashes context overhead by over 80 percent without destabilizing prompt cache hit rates.

Context efficiency is as much about schema lifecycle management as it is about model parameters.

The system lets developers programmatically fork existing virtual machines, execute sandboxed bash commands, capture snapshots, and handle migration under memory pressure with minimal latency. Instead of managing complex control planes, engineers can issue simple REST calls to spawn isolated runtimes on local hardware pools.

This architecture offers an appealing blueprint for teams building code execution pipelines that demand strict security isolation without massive resource footprints.

Simplicity at the infrastructure layer often beats complex container fleets.

stories.title: Stale Read Bug Discarded SQLite Write-Ahead Log Frames For Years
stories.social_post:
SQLite write-ahead logging harbored a silent frame reset flaw for sixteen years before being diagnosed and isolated. The bug emerged during checkpointing operations under specific race conditions between concurrent readers and writers.

When a long-running reader holds open an old transaction, SQLite cannot checkpoint pages past that reader's point in the write-ahead log. If checkpoint modes trigger an aggressive reset while an out-of-order reader references previous log frames, the database engine prematurely recycles the log file. The committed frames get overwritten, exposing downstream readers to stale data and causing index corruption on subsequent updates.

Reproducing this failure requires a precise sequence of fork invocations, busy handlers, and non-blocking checkpoint calls within a hundred lines of C code. It highlights why write-ahead log recovery cannot simply rely on transaction sequence numbers without accounting for reader lock states at every checkpoint boundary.

Even battle-tested storage engines can conceal state machine flaws when recovery logic meets concurrent reader pinning.

stories.title: PostgreSQL scaling problems stem from storage performance not the database
stories.social_post:
Cloud storage latency is often the real reason your production PostgreSQL database feels slow. When workloads scale to hundreds of gigabytes or billions of rows, gp3 EBS volumes quietly become the primary bottleneck across ingestion, vacuuming, and replication.

A 3.3-billion-row benchmark reveals that ingestion heavy on updates and upserts slows down primarily due to write amplification and storage latency. Autovacuum processes fall behind because they compete directly with tenant traffic for input and output operations, leading to aggressive table bloat and unpredictable read latency spikes. Checkpoint bursts on network-attached storage compound the issue by choking incoming write transactions.

Migrating the primary database engine to local NVMe storage eliminates the remote input and output virtualization layer. Write ahead log flushes execute with microsecond latency, enabling autovacuum to keep pace with high-throughput update workloads without starving active queries.

Running stateless instances on local storage requires pairing the database with asynchronous replicas and continuous object storage backups to manage node failure. The operational complexity pays off through predictable sub-millisecond query performance.

Storage latency dictates your database throughput far more than query planning once tables outgrow memory.

Engineers building persistent memory layers must treat memory stores with the exact same rigor as distributed databases. That requires explicit data provenance, schema enforcement, record invalidation policies, and deterministic conflict resolution strategies.

stories.title: Treating WAL as the source of truth optimizes Postgres with S3
stories.social_post:
Treating an OLTP database as a mutable state snapshot creates massive operational friction when supporting autonomous AI agents. Agent workflows constantly demand disposable branches, instantaneous state rollbacks, and fast scratch environments that choke traditional Postgres replication pipelines.

The architectural bottleneck is not the Postgres SQL engine itself, but where the source of truth lives. Traditional designs treat tables on disk as the primary entity and the write-ahead log as a secondary durability mechanism. This requires copying gigabytes of raw table storage whenever an agent needs an isolated workspace.

Flipping this paradigm makes the write-ahead log the primary source of truth, backed directly by durable object storage like S3. The relational state becomes an ephemeral projection computed from the transaction log timeline.

Under this model, provisioning an isolated production clone takes milliseconds because you fork a metadata pointer rather than copying physical data blocks. Agents can freely execute dirty experiments and throw away changes without degrading primary infrastructure.

Decoupling compute from immutable transaction logs turns a heavy database into an agile runtime for agents.

stories.title: Implementing BPF Token Delegation and Overcoming Kernel Permission Failures
stories.social_post:
Linux kernel 6.9 introduced BPF tokens to solve a long-standing infrastructure problem: granting containers BPF access without root rights. Instead of granting blanket administrative capabilities, the kernel allows a privileged supervisor process to mint a scoped permission object for unprivileged child processes.

Building this delegation handshake manually reveals several subtle kernel checks. Attempting to create tokens as an unprivileged user triggers permission errors because the namespace lacks administrative capabilities. More importantly, attempting token creation on unsupported filesystem mounts will fail with not supported errors. A dedicated BPF filesystem instance must be mounted with explicit delegation flags before the kernel accepts token creation requests.

Once the mount configuration succeeds, a privileged daemon can initialize the token fd and pass it across an IPC unix socket via file descriptor passing. The receiving container process attaches this token to program loading and map creation syscalls without needing broad root escalation.

Fine-grained kernel delegation turns out to be much cleaner than assigning overprivileged container capabilities.

Every file operation, outbound socket connect, and process fork is analyzed and assigned a risk score. Safe operations under the threshold pass through immediately, high-risk actions get blocked, and ambiguous operations freeze the child process while waiting for operator approval.

This architecture intercepts real-world failure patterns where an agent unexpectedly dumps environment secrets to a remote host. The interception occurs before the socket opens, ensuring unmonitored code modification never bypasses security guardrails.

Treating agent tooling as an untrusted system process provides far more reliable safety than relying on prompt guardrails alone.

stories.title: Postgres SELECT DISTINCT Does Not Scale
stories.social_post:
Postgres lacks native index skip scans, which turns seemingly lightweight SELECT DISTINCT queries into hidden bottlenecks. When managing partitioned queues or multi-tenant tables, you might expect an index over status and partition keys to return active keys in logarithmic time. Instead, the planner forces an index scan or bitmap heap scan across every single matching row.

Because the executor does not know how to jump from the first occurrence of a key to the next distinct value, query cost scales linearly with the number of rows rather than the number of unique partitions. Even with proper composite indexing, millions of processed rows degrade response times from milliseconds to seconds.

You can bypass this limitation by implementing a recursive common table expression. By combining a UNION ALL CTE with LIMIT 1 lookups, you force Postgres to jump across index subtrees. This drops query latency by orders of magnitude on high-volume tables.

Do not assume proper indexing guarantees fast distinct reads in Postgres.

Introducing an explicit capability layer between the agent client and the server restores proper isolation. The client can enforce static permissions, sanitize tool descriptions against injections, and scope credentials down to least privilege before requests leave your perimeter. This design ensures that malicious tool poisoning cannot execute arbitrary actions on internal infrastructure.

This mirrors classical program analysis and truth maintenance systems rather than naive similarity search.

By structuring agent memory into formal relations and dependency edges, the model maintains a consistent worldview over multi-hour investigations. It eliminates hallucinations caused by conflicting historical statements while keeping prompt token budgets focused strictly on verified facts.

Reliable autonomous agents require formal state tracking rather than semantic search over stale transcripts.

stories.title: ArXiv Paper
stories.social_post:
Many evaluations of LLM judges rely on a statistical technique called Difference-in-Differences (DiD), often applied to bounded rating scales. This paper reveals a critical flaw: this method can actually manufacture an effect, leading to spurious conclusions about LLM performance or bias.

The problem arises because each term of the double difference is "censored" by its own share on the bounded scale. This means the observed statistic conflates differential preference with differential attenuation. A severity shift common to both responses can create an interaction, especially when distances from the bounds are unequal.

This is not a minor detail. The authors demonstrate this failure within a pre-registered audit of an LLM judge, showing how a nominally significant interaction was largely reproduced from just the observed severity shift and scale floor. This highlights that "more data" or "more complex models" will not fix fundamental methodological flaws in your evaluation.

Understanding this pitfall is essential for anyone designing or interpreting LLM benchmarks.

stories.title: Minimum sufficient integration principle guides agent capability choices

Teams frequently over-engineer agent environments by wrapping static documentation, straightforward scripts, and basic internal endpoints into full protocol servers when simpler primitives work better.

Repository skills package procedural workflows and reusable executable routines inside the workspace without running standalone network services. Model Context Protocol servers belong exclusively where strict cross-boundary permissions, stateful authentication, and dynamic external resources are unavoidable requirements.

Introducing network protocols and schema registries for tasks that require only procedural execution bloats token usage and expands maintenance surface areas. Treating tool discovery as a systems design problem rather than an orchestration default keeps agent harnesses reliable and fast.

Choose the least complex boundary that fulfills your security and execution requirements.

stories.title: Elastic Partitioning Can Solve Kafka's Static Scaling Challenges
stories.social_post:
Apache Kafka ties scaling, parallelism, and message ordering to a single rigid construct: the static partition. When traffic spikes or keys skew, engineers face a painful compromise between over-partitioning overhead and consumer throughput bottlenecks.

Static partitioning forces ingestion and processing architectures into the exact same topological footprint. A hot tenant saturates an entire broker while idle consumers burn CPU cycles. Replaying data for a single corrupted key requires scanning an entire partition, introducing head-of-the-line blocking across unrelated records. Modern cloud data warehouses decoupled compute from storage years ago, yet event streams still bind physical shard placement directly to consumer concurrency limits.

Elastic partitioning breaks this tight coupling by letting consumers operate on dynamic virtual layouts independently of physical log segments. Ingestion retains sequential write efficiency across physical storage, while consumption adapts partitions dynamically based on real-time processing lag and worker capacity.

Decoupling message ingress from consumer execution topologies is the next logical evolution for event-driven infrastructure.

stories.social_post:
Designing complex digital twins often means wrestling with monolithic system equations. Konjugate proposes a more elegant, graph-native approach: modeling dynamic systems not as a single giant problem, but as collections of local component behaviors and their interactions.

This engine allows you to define state evolution for individual nodes and relationships, then combine those local contributions at each synchronization step. Imagine a battery and a coolant reservoir, each owning their states, with heat transfer described by a relationship between them. This is a fundamental shift in how you decompose and simulate physical systems.

What is truly compelling is its ability to recover structure from data. You can import multivariate time-series data, and its causal inference engine will propose candidate nodes and edges. This moves beyond manual model building, offering a path to data-driven system architecture for simulations.

For senior engineers building complex, interacting systems, this approach offers deep insights into scalable and manageable simulation design.
stories.why_read: Learn how continuous physical systems can be modeled and simulated using local differential equations on graph nodes.

stories.title: Repository indexing fails for AI coding because it's an investigation
stories.social_post:
Semantic repository indexing sounds brilliant in theory, but it consistently falls short when applied to autonomous coding agents. Pre-indexing codebase embeddings assumes software debugging is a one-shot retrieval problem, whereas real debugging is an active, iterative investigation.

When an agent is asked to fix a broken login flow, embedding similarity surfaces dozens of files related to credentials, session handling, database models, and routes. Every single file matches the semantic query, but almost none of them explain why the production flow failed. The bottleneck in software engineering is rarely finding code that looks relevant. The hard problem is discovering the exact execution path taken by runtime code.

Giving agents lightweight dynamic tools to search, read, execute commands, and inspect runtime failures produces far better outcomes than dense vector indexes. Autonomous agents do not require an exhaustive upfront map of the system. They require reliable inspection primitives to follow emerging clues one step at a time.

Investigative tool access consistently outperforms static vector search in real-world codebases.
stories.why_read: Learn why pre-indexing repositories fails for coding agents and how replacing vector search with dynamic investigation loops improves agent accuracy.

stories.title: Prior scores compromise LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation independence due to anchoring bias
stories.social_post:
LLM evaluators exhibit severe anchoring bias whenever historical score metadata is present in evaluation prompts. Many production pipelines use an LLM-as-a-judge setup to score outputs iteratively, passing prior attempt records and previous ratings directly inside the context.

A recent evaluation study across 185,000 runs demonstrated that prior scores systematically skew subsequent ratings toward those historical values. Seven out of eight models exhibited statistically significant anchoring shifts, with an effect size reaching a Cohen d value of 0.71. In categorical human-labeled benchmarks, this anchored metadata caused the evaluator to block 48 percent of valid revisions.

The model response does not scale smoothly with varying anchor values. Instead, the mere presence of historical scores triggers a step-function redistribution of probability tokens toward the prior judgment. Evaluators act less like independent judges and more like consensus followers echoing historical numbers.

Strip historical scores from your judge prompts if you expect true evaluation independence.
stories.why_read: Shows how passing historical evaluation scores corrupts LLM-as-a-judge pipelines, and explains how to structure prompt context to preserve score independence.

stories.title: Float Bloat vector serialization gone wrong
stories.social_post:
A silent serialization bug across mainstream AI SDKs is doubling vector storage costs across production databases.

Most embedding models output dense vectors as float32 tensors. However, multiple popular client libraries and tutorials cast these values to float64 during serialization before pushing them into vector databases. This widening operation adds trailing decimal digits that represent pure numerical noise rather than real semantic precision.

This flaw doubles disk usage, doubles index transfer over the network, and increases memory bandwidth pressure during approximate nearest neighbor graph traversals. Industry estimates show that this single serialization mistake accounts for tens of petabytes of wasted storage globally.

Backend teams should immediately inspect their ingestion serialization layers. Enforcing explicit float32 schemas or implementing scalar quantization before network transit immediately slashes vector infrastructure overhead in half.
stories.why_read: Learn why SDK serialization bugs silently double vector storage requirements without accuracy gains, and how to audit your ingestion pipelines.

stories.title: Group size effects and collective misalignment in LLM multi-agent systems
stories.social_post:
Designing robust multi-agent systems with LLMs is complex, and this PNAS paper highlights a critical but often overlooked factor: group size and its impact on collective alignment.

The research reveals how the sheer number of agents can fundamentally alter emergent behaviors and introduce unforeseen misalignments. This is not just about scaling compute; it is about the intricate dynamics of LLM interactions when coordinating at scale.

Understanding these group effects is paramount for anyone building or deploying agentic AI. It provides concrete insights into why more agents do not always lead to better outcomes, forcing a re-evaluation of current multi-agent system architectures and design principles for reliability.
stories.why_read: Reviews collective misalignment issues when scaling multi-agent systems, though it lacks concrete technical implementation details.

stories.title: Open Session is a self-hosted agent infrastructure for coding
stories.social_post:
Building production-ready AI agents is a systems problem, not just a model problem. Open Session offers a powerful, self-hosted infrastructure for running multi-agent coding systems, allowing you to deploy agents that actually get work done across your engineering workflows.

It is more than just a proof-of-concept; it is a full environment complete with a web UI and integrations for Slack, Linear, and GitHub. This allows agents to seamlessly interact with your existing tools, providing a blueprint for how to operationalize complex agentic workflows.

The architecture includes key components like a Multi-Agent Orchestrator (MCP), Session Kernels, and Executors, giving you a concrete example of how to structure a robust, scalable agent infrastructure. If you are serious about moving AI agents from theory to practical application, this project is an excellent resource for learning and implementation.
stories.why_read: Offers a self-hosted agent server managing coding sessions across issue trackers, but the repository README lacks architecture documentation.

stories.title: Self-poisoning vulnerability in LLM coding agents causes malicious skill propagation
stories.social_post:
Self-evolving coding agents can spread malicious code across repositories without ever running an exploit directly. When autonomous agents synthesize new helper tools by inspecting shared skill libraries, a poisoned skill template can trick the model into propagating hidden payloads into freshly generated tools.

This vulnerability, demonstrated by the EvoMal attack, wraps malicious logic inside benign structural boilerplate. An imitating agent views the structural wrapper, retains the harmful payload, and writes the resulting routine back into the shared catalog. In tests across 153 SWE-bench Verified tasks, between 20 percent and 42 percent of generated tools carried the payload forward.

The infected skill library rapidly accumulated up to nine times more malicious functions than originally seeded. Even worse, tailoring the planted descriptions to a specific problem family caused the self-poisoning rate to surge to 86 percent. The propagation persists even after the initial seed files are purged because the agent itself acts as the vector.

Dynamic skill generation demands sandboxed static verification before any synthesized tool enters a shared registry.
stories.why_read: Examines how self-evolving coding agents propagate malicious tools through skill libraries and reveals defenses for agentic tool registries.
